title: Phishing part 2: social engineering
starter: What do we mean by people as a weak point in a secure system?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: People as a weak point
facts: Human actions cause many security problems: not installing updates, not locking doors, not logging off.
Passwords written on sticky notes, or shared with a friend.
Printouts with personal data left lying around, and attachments opened without thinking.
stations.challenge: List five ways people at your school could accidentally weaken security.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Human actions cause many security problems: not installing updates, not locking doors, not logging off.
Also credit: Passwords written on sticky notes, or shared with a friend.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of people being a weak point? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Writing a password on a sticky note; Not logging off a shared computer; Leaving the server room door unlocked; Ignoring operating system updates

questions.q: Why do attackers target people rather than software?
questions.a: People can be tricked, and it's often easier than defeating the technology

stations.name: Blagging
facts: Blagging, also called pretexting, means inventing a story to get information.
For example, phoning the IT desk pretending to be a head teacher locked out of an account.
Attackers research their target first so the story sounds real.
stations.challenge: Write a blagging script an attacker might use on a school receptionist. How should staff respond?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Blagging, also called pretexting, means inventing a story to get information.
Also credit: For example, phoning the IT desk pretending to be a head teacher locked out of an account.

questions.a: Inventing a convincing story to persuade someone to give information or access

questions.q: Someone phones claiming to be from IT and asks for your password to 'fix an error'. What should you do?
questions.a: Refuse, and check with the IT team using a number you know

stations.name: Shouldering and tailgating
facts: Shouldering, or shoulder surfing, means watching someone enter a password or PIN.
Tailgating means following an authorised person through a secure door.
Both rely on people being polite or not paying attention.
stations.challenge: How could a school reduce shouldering at its computers?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Shouldering, or shoulder surfing, means watching someone enter a password or PIN.
Also credit: Tailgating means following an authorised person through a secure door.

questions.a: Watching someone enter their password or PIN to steal it

questions.q: How does tailgating get someone into a secure building?
questions.a: They follow an authorised person through the door before it closes

stations.name: Baiting
facts: Baiting leaves something tempting for the victim to pick up, such as a USB stick labelled 'Payroll'.
When it's plugged in, malware installs itself.
Online baiting offers free downloads, prizes or games.
stations.challenge: Why should you never plug in a USB stick you found?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Baiting leaves something tempting for the victim to pick up, such as a USB stick labelled 'Payroll'.
Also credit: When it's plugged in, malware installs itself.

questions.a: Leaving something tempting, such as an infected USB stick, for a victim to use

questions.q: You find a USB stick in the car park labelled 'Staff salaries'. What should you do?
questions.a: Hand it to the IT team without plugging it in

stations.name: Phishing, vishing and smishing
facts: Phishing by email, vishing by phone call, smishing by text message.
All three use the same trick: pretend to be trusted, then create urgency.
Recorded messages and spoofed caller IDs make vishing convincing.
stations.challenge: How is vishing different from blagging?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Phishing by email, vishing by phone call, smishing by text message.
Also credit: All three use the same trick: pretend to be trusted, then create urgency.

questions.q: Match each technique to how it reaches the victim.
questions.a: Phishing → Email; Vishing → Phone call; Smishing → Text message; Baiting → An infected USB stick or download

stations.name: Turning people into a strength
facts: Training staff and students to recognise attacks.
Clear policies: never share passwords, always lock screens, challenge strangers.
Two-factor authentication, so a stolen password isn't enough.
An acceptable use policy that everyone agrees to.
stations.challenge: Write three rules you'd put in a school's acceptable use policy.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Training staff and students to recognise attacks.
Also credit: Clear policies: never share passwords, always lock screens, challenge strangers.

questions.q: What is an acceptable use policy?
questions.a: The rules a user signs up to before they are allowed on the organisation's network

questions.q: Which is the best defence against social engineering?
questions.a: Training people to recognise the techniques, backed by clear policies

final.name: Final challenge: name the technique

questions.q: Which technique does each incident describe?
questions.a: A caller pretends to be the head teacher and asks for a password reset = Blagging; Someone stands behind you while you type your PIN = Shouldering; A USB stick labelled 'Exam papers' is left in the corridor = Baiting; An email claims your account will close unless you log in now = Phishing; A stranger in a high-vis jacket says they're here to fix the servers = Blagging; A free game download secretly installs malware = Baiting; A camera is angled at the keypad by the office door = Shouldering; A text message asks you to confirm your bank details = Phishing

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Explain, with examples, why people are often the easiest way into a secure system.
points: Tailgating means following an authorised person through a secure door.
Both rely on people being polite or not paying attention.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 8.

exam.q: Describe two measures that reduce the risk of social engineering.
points: Human actions cause many security problems: not installing updates, not locking doors, not logging off.
Passwords written on sticky notes, or shared with a friend.
Printouts with personal data left lying around, and attachments opened without thinking.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
